lede: A matrix is a rectangle of numbers kept together so it can be worked with as one object. Adding and subtracting behave exactly as you would guess. Multiplying does not: it pairs a row with a column, and the order you multiply in changes the answer.
can: Add, subtract and scale matrices entry by entry, and say when you cannot
Multiply two matrices by pairing each row with each column
Decide from the shapes whether a product exists, and what shape it will be

md:
A matrix is written inside brackets and described by its shape: **rows first, then columns**. Here $A$ and $B$ are $2 \times 2$, and $C$ is $2 \times 3$.
The shape is not decoration. It decides what you are allowed to do: two matrices can only be added if they are the same shape, and can only be multiplied if the shapes fit together in one particular way.

prompt: One tap to begin. The matrix $C$ shown above has two rows and three columns. What is its shape called?
explain: Rows first, then columns, so $C$ is $2 \times 3$. Getting that order the wrong way round is what makes the multiplication rule look impossible later.

md:
These three are the easy ones. To add, add the entries in matching positions. To subtract, subtract them. To multiply by a number, multiply **every** entry by it.
The only rule is shape: $A + B$ works because both are $2 \times 2$, but $A + C$ does not exist at all, because the third column of $C$ has nothing in $A$ to pair with.

prompt: In the addition shown above, $A$ has $2$ in row 2, column 1 and $B$ has $-1$ in the same place. What is the entry in row 2, column 1 of $A + B$?
explain: $2 + (-1) = 1$. Every entry of a sum comes from the one position it sits in.

text: 2. Multiplying: a row meets a column

md:
Multiplication does not work position by position. To find the entry in **row $i$, column $j$** of $AB$, take row $i$ of $A$ and column $j$ of $B$, multiply term by term and add.
Why not entry by entry? Because a matrix stands for a whole set of combinations at once, and each row of the first has to meet every column of the second.

title: Why entry by entry is not multiplication
md: Multiplying matching entries would leave each number of the answer resting on one number from each matrix. Row by column makes every entry rest on a whole row and a whole column, which is what lets one matrix stand for a system of equations later in this unit.

prompt: Using $A$ and $B$ from this lesson, row 2 of $A$ is $2$, $4$ and column 1 of $B$ is $5$, $-1$. What is the entry in row 2, column 1 of $AB$?
explain: $(2)(5) + (4)(-1) = 6$. Term by term along the row and down the column, then add.

md:
Write the two shapes side by side. The product exists only when the **inner** two numbers match, and then the **outer** two give the shape of the answer.
So $2 \times 2$ times $2 \times 3$ works and gives a $2 \times 3$ answer. The other way round, $2 \times 3$ times $2 \times 2$, has inner numbers $3$ and $2$, so that product does not exist.

prompt: Using the shape rule shown above, what shape is the product of a $2 \times 2$ matrix and a $2 \times 3$ matrix, in that order?
explain: The inner numbers are both $2$, so the product exists, and the outer numbers $2$ and $3$ give its shape.

text: 4. Two things that catch people out

md:
**The order matters.** $AB$ and $BA$ are different matrices, and often only one of them exists. Never swap them to make the arithmetic easier.
**Squaring means multiplying.** $A^{2}$ is $A \times A$, worked out row by column. It is not the matrix you get by squaring each entry, and that is the slip examiners report most often on this topic.

title: Summer 2024, Unit 1, Question 7
md: Candidates who squared each entry instead of multiplying the matrix by itself lost the whole part. The same slip is reported in Summer 2019 and Summer 2023, so it is worth one deliberate check: write the multiplication out before you start.

title: Multiplying Matrices 2x2 by 2x2 - Corbettmaths
why: The row-by-column sweep worked through slowly on several pairs of matrices.

prompt: For the matrix $A$ in this lesson, $A^{2}$ means $A \times A$. Row 1 of $A$ is $3$, $-1$ and column 1 of $A$ is $3$, $2$. What is the entry in row 1, column 1 of $A^{2}$?
explain: $(3)(3) + (-1)(2) = 7$. Squaring the entry alone would give $9$, which is a different matrix.

md:
Add, subtract and scale entry by entry, and say when the shapes forbid it.
Multiply by pairing each row of the first with each column of the second.
Use the shape rule to decide whether a product exists and what shape it is.
Treat $AB$ and $BA$ as different matrices.
Work out $A^{2}$ as $A \times A$, never by squaring the entries.

Matrix arithmetic is a short question, usually $4$ to $6$ marks across two or three parts: a scalar multiple or a sum, then a product. It opened the paper in Summer 2019 and Summer 2025. The first mark is the row-by-column working written out; the last is every entry right. Stuck on a product? Write the shapes down first — they tell you whether to start at all, and how many entries the answer needs.
